title: Speech and breath argue about who is greatest (1.2)
hook: the senses quarrel over which of them matters most, and they settle it by leaving the body one at a time

segments.voice: Yesterday: the udgitha, om, the essence of essences: earth, water, plants, person, speech, verse, chant, om. Your line was the essence.

Sooner or later, every team has this argument. The one who talks to the clients says the company runs on them. The one who builds the product says nothing exists without them. The planner says without a plan it's all chaos. Everyone is a little bit right, and nobody wants to hear it. The Chandogya Upanishad tells the same fight, only the team is inside your own body: speech, the eye, the ear, the mind and the breath, arguing over which of them is the greatest. The way they settle it is brilliant, and a little brutal.
screen: `EVERY TEAM HAS THIS ARGUMENT.` → `THE TEAM IS YOUR BODY.` → `WHO IS THE GREATEST?`

segments.voice: They go to Prajapati, the lord of creatures, and ask him to judge. His test: the greatest is the one whose leaving makes the body worst off. So they take turns walking out. Speech leaves for a whole year. Back again, it asks: how did you manage without me? Like someone who can't speak, the others say. We breathed, we saw, we heard, we thought. We got by. The eye leaves for a year, and they get by like someone who can't see. The ear leaves, and they live like someone who can't hear. The mind leaves, and they live, the text says, like small children whose minds haven't grown yet. Each time, the body carries on. Then breath gets ready to go. And here's the picture that makes the story stick: as a strong horse, pulling away, tears up the pegs it was tethered to, the breath begins to tear up all the others with it. Speech, eye, ear and mind come running. Stay, they say. You're the greatest of us. That full story sits in chapter five of the Chandogya. In chapter one, the passage the outline points to, a shorter story makes the same point: gods and demons fight, and the demons spoil speech, eye, ear and mind with evil. But when they strike the breath in the mouth, the chief breath, they shatter like a clod of earth thrown at a rock. In both places, breath holds the rest. And chapter five ends by saying people don't call the senses speech, eyes, ears and minds. They call them all pranas, breaths.
screen: `PRAJAPATI'S TEST: WHO CAN LEAVE?` · `SPEECH, EYE, EAR, MIND: THE BODY GETS BY.` · `THE HORSE TEARS UP ITS PEGS.` · `THE SENSES ARE CALLED BREATHS.` · then, large: `STAY. YOU'RE THE GREATEST.`

segments.voice: Give the senses the day off: let your eyes close, let the room's sounds fall to the background, stay silent, and let thoughts drift past without chasing them. Then notice what's still going without being asked, in and out, the one the others ran back to. Just keep it company.
Prana, life-breath. When breath prepares to leave the body, like a strong horse tearing up its tethering pegs, speech, eye, ear and mind come running, calling it the greatest of them all.
Your line: breath wins. The others can step out for a year; breath holds them all. Day three hundred thirty-three, done.

howItsDone: Many Hindus practice pranayama, the regulation of breath, as part of daily worship and yoga; teachers sometimes tell this story of breath as the chief of the senses alongside it.

fork.setup: you're Prajapati. the senses want you to say which of them is greatest. how do you judge?
options: let each one leave the body for a while, and see whose absence hurts most.
say they're all equal and send them home.
fork.reveal: the test is absence. speech, eye, ear and mind each leave for a year and the body manages. when breath starts to go, everything comes with it.

original.note: Sanskrit prāṇa: breath, life-breath. the Chandogya says the senses are all called prāṇas, after their chief.

trapdoor: what you thought: a fable about the body's parts, like a children's story.
what it means: a test of absence. every sense can leave and the body carries on, except breath, which holds all the others.
what a scholar hears: the full dispute is Chandogya 5.1 (and Brihadaranyaka 6.1); 1.2 tells the gods-and-demons version, where evil can't touch the chief breath.

chat.says: In that old Upanishad story, why does breath beat speech and the mind?
options: Each sense left and the body got by. When breath began to go, it pulled the rest.
Because speech lied to Prajapati, so he punished it and crowned breath instead.
Because Prajapati picked breath as his favorite without testing any of them.
chat.meaning: Under Prajapati's test, speech, eye, ear and mind each left for a year and the body carried on. Breath leaving tore up all the rest.

Prajapati.meaning: the lord of creatures, who judges the senses' dispute
